title: Filling the gap in Vitex-associated gall mite evolution: characterization of Aceria vitecicola (Kikuti) from Japan and its relationship with A. massalongoi (Canestrini)
content:
Abstract
Six Aceria species are known to induce galls on Vitex (Lamiaceae) worldwide; however, their phylogenetic relationships and evolutionary history remain entirely unexplored. Among these, Aceria vitecicola induces pouch galls on Vitex rotundifolia in Japan. Based on the external morphological similarities between the galls of A. vitecicola and those induced by A. massalongoi on V. agnus-castus, these Vitex-associated mites were presumed to share a close phylogenetic affinity. Here, we histologically characterized the A. vitecicola-induced galls and inferred the molecular phylogenetic position of A. vitecicola within Aceria. Histological analyses revealed that A. vitecicola induces complex galls featuring specialized nutritive tissue with enlarged, occasionally binucleate nuclei—traits similar to A. massalongoi galls. Molecular phylogenies based on COI and ITS1 markers consistently placed A. vitecicola as a sister taxon to A. massalongoi. Our molecular dating revealed a deep genetic divergence between these taxa during the early Palaeogene, aligning with the macroevolutionary rise of the family Lamiaceae. These results support a model of host-constrained diversification, suggesting that gall-inducing traits are phylogenetically conserved within this lineage. This study underscores deep-time host–parasite associations and highlights the need for broader sampling across Eurasia, alongside divergence dating of the Vitex hosts, to fully elucidate their evolutionary history.
